title: What terrors do we invent?
source_text: Ποῖα δὲ παντοδαπὰ ἐπισπώμεθα ἢ τίνα συμπλάσσομεν δείματα, ὡς ἀναποδείκτως γράφει ὁ Κέλσος, παραστησάτω ὁ βουλόμενος. εἰ μὴ ἄρα τὴν περὶ δικαστοῦ θεοῦ καὶ δικαζομένων ἀνθρώπων ἐφ᾿ οἷς ἔπραξαν πᾶσι διδασκαλίαν μετὰ κατασκευῆς ποικίλης, πῇ μὲν τῆς ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν πῇ δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ εἰκότος λόγου, δείματα βούλεται λέγειν ὁ Κέλσος συμπεπλασμένα. καίτοι γε (φίλη γὰρ ἡ ἀλήθεια) φησὶ πρὸς τοῖς τελευταίοις ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι μήτε τούτοις εἴη μήτ᾿ ἐμοὶ μήτε ἄλλῳ τινὶ ἀνθρώπων ἀποθέσθαι τὸ περὶ τοῦ κολασθήσεσθαι τοὺς ἀδίκους καὶ γερῶν ἀξιωθήσεσθαι τοὺς δικαίους δόγμα. ποῖα οὖν δείματα. ἐὰν ἀνέλῃς τὸν περὶ κολάσεως λόγον. συμπλάττοντες ἐπισπώμεθα τοὺς ἀνθρώπους; ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὰν λέγῃ ὅτι τὰ τοῦ παλαιοῦ λόγου παρακούσματα συμπλάττοντες τούτοις προκαταυλοῦμεν καὶ προκατηχοῦμεν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ὡς οἱ τοὺς κορυβαντιζομένους περιβομβοῦντες, φήσομεν πρὸς αὐτόν· ποίου παλαιοῦ λόγου παρακούσματα; εἴτε γὰρ τοῦ Ἑλληνικοῦ, καὶ διδάξαντος περὶ τῶν ὑπὸ γῆν δικαστηρίων. εἴτε τοῦ Ἰουδαϊκοῦ, μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων καὶ περὶ τῆς ἑξῆς τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ ζωῆς προφητεύσαντος, οὐκ ἂν ἔχοι παραστῆσαι ὅτι ἡμεῖς ἐν παρακούσμασι γενόμενοι τῆς ἀληθείας, ὅσοι γε πειρώμεθα μετὰ λόγου πιστεύειν, πρὸς τὰ τοιαῦτα ζῶμεν δόγματα.
pass_a_gloss: What all-sorts (παντοδαπά) do we draw in (ἐπισπώμεθα) or what terrors (δείματα) do we fabricate (συμπλάσσομεν), as Celsus writes without proof (ἀναποδείκτως), let him who wishes present (παραστησάτω). Unless then Celsus wishes to call fabricated terrors the teaching (διδασκαλία) about God as judge (δικαστοῦ θεοῦ) and men being judged (δικαζομένων) for all they did, with varied establishment, partly from the Scriptures (γραφῶν), partly from likely reasoning (εἰκότος λόγου). And yet Celsus says toward the last that 'may it be neither for these nor for me nor for any other of men to put away (ἀποθέσθαι) the doctrine (δόγμα) about the unjust (ἀδίκους) being punished (κολασθήσεσθαι) and the just (δικαίους) being deemed worthy of rewards (γερῶν ἀξιωθήσεσθαι)'. What terrors then, if you remove (ἀνέλῃς) the account about punishment (κόλασις), fabricating do we draw men? But also when he says that 'fabricating mishearings (παρακούσματα) of the ancient account (παλαιοῦ λόγου) we pipe beforehand (προκαταυλοῦμεν) with these and instruct/din beforehand (προκατηχοῦμεν) men, as those booming around (περιβομβοῦντες) the Corybant-frenzied (κορυβαντιζομένους)', we shall say to him: mishearings of what ancient account? For whether of the Greek, which also taught about the under-earth law-courts (ὑπὸ γῆν δικαστηρίων), or the Jewish, prophesying among others also about the life after this life, he could not present that we, having come to be in mishearings of the truth, at least as many as try to believe with reason, live toward such doctrines.

lemmas.lemma: for truth is dear, φίλη ἡ ἀλήθεια

pass_b_english: What are these “all sorts of things” by which we draw people, or what are the “terrors” we “invent,” as Celsus writes without any proof? Let anyone who wishes show it. Unless, perhaps, Celsus means to call “invented terrors” the teaching about God as judge and about men being judged for all they have done, a teaching established with varied proof, partly from the Scriptures and partly from reasonable argument.

And yet (for truth is dear) Celsus says, near the end of his work, “May neither these people, nor I, nor any other human being cast off the doctrine that the unjust will be punished and the just counted worthy of rewards.” What terrors, then, if you take away the teaching on punishment, do we invent to draw people in?

Again, when he says that we invent “misheard versions of the ancient account” and with these pipe to people beforehand and fill their ears beforehand, “like those who make a din around people in the frenzy of the Corybantic rites,” we shall say to him: misheard versions of what ancient account? For whether it is the Greek account, which also taught about the courts beneath the earth, or the Jewish one, which among other things prophesied also about the life that follows this life, he could not show that we live by such doctrines as men who have misheard the truth, at least those of us who try to believe with reason.

choices.choice: The opening question takes up Celsus's words (παντοδαπὰ ἐπισπώμενοι, δείματα συμπλάσσοντες), marked as quoted words though Origen recasts them in the first person. 'φίλη γὰρ ἡ ἀλήθεια' rendered '(for truth is dear)'; it may echo Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1096a16, not certain enough to cite. 'πρὸς τοῖς τελευταίοις' = near the end of Celsus's book (compare Against Celsus 8.48-49). Celsus's wish (μήτε ... εἴη ... ἀποθέσθαι, optative) rendered 'May neither ... cast off'. The second charge is given by Origen in indirect speech in the first person plural ('we pipe'), so it is rendered as indirect speech, with quotation marks only on the phrases that are plainly Celsus's own wording, so that 'we' is not put into Celsus's mouth. 'παρακούσματα' = 'mishearings, misunderstandings'. 'προκατηχοῦμεν' (literally 'sound in the ears beforehand') rendered 'fill their ears beforehand'. The Corybantic image may recall Plato, Crito 54d, but is Celsus's own and uncertain; not cited. 'courts beneath the earth' recalls Plato's judgment myths (Gorgias 523-524; Republic 10.614c), not cited as no text is quoted. Judgment 'for all they have done' may echo Romans 2:6 / 2 Corinthians 5:10 (possible allusion, not cited inline). Staging punctuation (full stops after δείματα, λόγον, δικαστηρίων) ignored as breaking single sentences.

Corybantic charge: the whole indirect, first-person-plural report (ὅτι ... προκαταυλοῦμεν) had been set in quotation marks, which put 'we' into Celsus's mouth; now rendered as indirect speech with quotation marks only on Celsus's own phrases.
Added 'also' for καί in 'which also taught about the courts beneath the earth' (καὶ διδάξαντος), previously omitted.
Translator note corrected to match the English ('May neither ... cast off'; the note had 'ever', which the English does not have) and to explain the indirect-speech handling.
